claims.text: Al0.5NbTa0.8Ti1.5V0.2Zr is a refractory high-entropy alloy.
Al0.5NbTa0.8Ti1.5V0.2Zr can be processed to exhibit a ductile–brittle–ductile transition.
The initial cast, HIPed, homogenized, and slowly cooled alloy has a continuous ordered B2 matrix with discrete BCC precipitates.
The initial continuous-B2 condition is brittle, exhibiting only 4.7% compressive fracture strain.
A continuous ordered B2 matrix intrinsically restricts dislocation motion and thereby causes brittleness.
Solution treatment at 1400 °C for 20 minutes followed by water quenching breaks down the continuous B2 matrix and produces a weakly ordered BCC structure containing nanoscale B2 regions.
The solutionized condition can attain more than 60% compressive ductility at room temperature, although its yield strength decreases to 1065 MPa.

Annealing the solutionized alloy at 600 °C for 120 hours followed by water quenching produces an inverted microstructure consisting of a continuous disordered BCC matrix and discrete approximately 50 nm B2 precipitates.
Making disordered BCC the continuous phase promotes dislocation mobility.
Discrete B2 precipitates provide precipitation strengthening without significantly impeding plasticity.
The inverted microstructure restores ductility at both room temperature and 600 °C.
The inverted alloy should achieve approximately 38% compressive strain at room temperature.
The processed alloy should exhibit anomalous strengthening, with yield strength at 600 °C comparable to or greater than its room-temperature yield strength.
Room-temperature and 600 °C uniaxial compression tests are appropriate for evaluating the alloy states.
Conventional alloys typically exhibit a narrow temper-embrittlement window because of continuous brittle phases.
High-entropy alloys can avoid temper embrittlement when processing favors a continuous ductile phase.
The desired inversion and transition require finely tuned temperature, time, and cooling rate, and processing deviations may prevent them.
